note: The principle (shortened red-cell survival falsely lowers HbA1c regardless of assay method) is confirmed, with NGSP examples "recovery from acute blood loss, hemolytic anemia". But the entry's list goes beyond what the sources say: (1) transfusion: NGSP gives no direction; it appears only as a reason for caution in HbSS/HbCC/HbSC; (2) HbSS and HbSC: NGSP says "must be interpreted with caution", direction not stated (and ADA 2026 Section 6 says A1C cannot be measured at all in HbSS); (3) malaria: not mentioned on the NGSP page. Malaria appears in WHO 2011 (https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK304271/): "The most common important factors worldwide affecting HbA1c levels are haemoglobinopathies (depending on the assay employed), certain anaemias, and disorders associated with accelerated red cell turnover such as malaria", again without a stated direction. WHO 2011 Annex 1 lists under Decreased HbA1c "decreased erythrocyte life span: haemoglobinopathies, splenomegaly, rheumatoid arthritis or drugs"; malaria and transfusion are not in that table. Reword so that transfusion, HbSS/HbSC and malaria are "unreliable, interpret with caution / use glucose" rather than "falsely lowers".
